opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Clark is honestly one of the main reasons I had such a good PhD experience.

The first thing is that he gave me a lot of freedom. I started out in formal methods and verification, which is his home area, but over time I became more and more interested in machine learning systems and large language models. A lot of advisors would push you to stay in their lane, because that's where they can help most and where their funding is. Clark never did that. He said, if this is what you're excited about, go do it, and I'll support you however I can. That trust meant a lot, especially early on when I wasn't sure myself whether switching directions was a good idea.

The second thing is that he really cares about students as people, not just as producers of papers. If you were stuck, or burned out, or worried about your career, you could talk to him openly. He'd listen first and then give very practical advice. He never made me feel I had to prove myself every week to deserve his time.

And third, he's very rigorous. Coming from verification, he cares about getting things exactly right: precise definitions, clear claims, no hand-waving. Even after I moved into more empirical, systems-style work, that habit stayed with me. When you build something like an inference engine, correctness and careful thinking still matter a lot, and I learned that mindset from him.

So I'd say it's the combination: freedom to explore, real care for his students, and a high standard of rigor. That's rare, and I feel very lucky to have had it.

fable-5.1.text:
Clark was unusual in that he never tried to make me into a copy of himself. A lot of advisors have a research agenda, and students become hands for that agenda. Clark would sit with me, ask what I actually found interesting, and then help me figure out whether there was a real problem underneath it. When I wanted to move from more theoretical work toward systems and later toward large models, he did not resist. He asked hard questions, but he let me go.

The second thing is that he was genuinely available. If I sent a draft at midnight, I would often have detailed comments the next morning. Not just "looks good," but line by line, where the argument was weak, where a claim needed evidence. That kind of attention teaches you what rigor feels like, because you see it applied to your own work over and over.

And he was honest without being discouraging. If an idea was not good, he would say so plainly, but he would also explain why, and usually point toward the version of the idea that might work. I never left a meeting feeling smaller. I left with more to do, which is a very different feeling.

Finally, he treated the students as colleagues early. He would introduce us to people at conferences as collaborators, push us to give the talks, and let us take credit publicly. That gave me confidence before I probably deserved it, and that confidence turned out to matter a lot when I started doing open-source and infrastructure work later, where you have to put things out in front of people constantly.

His guidance helped me develop that judgment and become a more independent researcher.
